name: Ivan Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; this is confidential, and your name won't go in our findings. Tell me about a usual shift at the utility.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 43, a junior lineworker. I check the digital weather and road closures on my phone before I leave, then at the depot I test the radio and lay out the grounding kit with the crew. Most days I ride out to repair a fault, carry cable, and learn by watching the lead.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy in the work, and what part follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like figuring out how a fault travelled through a feeder and seeing the houses come back on. I sometimes keep thinking about a missed check after I get home, especially with my partner Nadia and our two children, ages 6 and 9, waiting for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like my present week with a few easier screens. I use an AI route assistant for road closures and muddy access, but I still want the crew to check the pole before we set up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the route assistant for mud and closures, but I still check the pole with my own eyes. It saves a call to dispatch, not the careful work at the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think this small change removes my field job because the physical work stays much the same. My pay is still low for our mortgage and children's costs, so a week with no overtime would pinch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the grounding and cable-handling steps on real callouts. I already put small amounts into a separate account when my pay permits, and I would keep doing that after the screen changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job itself, but anxious about having less than a month's expenses saved. That worry was here before anybody started talking about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the route assistant for, and what do you check another way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to flag a washed-out lane or a gate that blocks the service truck. I still phone the dispatcher if the screen and a neighbour's report don't agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that thin savings account change about the choices you can make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't afford to leave a paid shift for an unpaid course, even if it sounds useful. I have to look for training the company pays for and schedule it around the roster.

say: I use the route assistant for **mud and closures**, but I still inspect the pole.
I tell the crew a screen saves a dispatch call, not **site checks**.
think: I don't expect this small change to remove my **field job**.
I still worry that one week without overtime would strain our **mortgage budget**.
do: Keep practising the **grounding steps** on real repair callouts.
Put spare pay into a **separate savings account** when bills permit.
feel: I feel secure about the task, but **thin savings** keep my household anxious.
S0.quote: I use the route assistant for mud and closures, but I still check the pole with my own eyes.
fieldNote: He adopts digital route help quickly but keeps a **physical site check** in the work sequence.
His job confidence sits alongside a **limited cash buffer** and a fixed mortgage.

steps.text: Keep practising grounding and cable-handling steps on callouts
Transfer leftover pay to a separate savings account after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could use AI to predict which feeder needs a crew first and shorten the calls we wait for. We would still have to look up and see if a branch or damaged insulator is actually there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a clean diagram doesn't show the loose branch on the actual road. A crew has to make the site safe before anyone climbs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see experienced people getting more work while the company leaves junior names off the roster. If routine inspections take less time, there may be fewer calls and my low pay gives me little room to absorb lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the approved AI route tool every day and learn its new features from the senior crew, since I already use it for access notes. I would ask for an additional paid field qualification and track whether our callout hours are falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about my roster, though I can learn tools quickly when they help the job. The mortgage is due whether the app gives us five callouts or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as a sign that the new planning system is reducing your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company cancels our regular inspection days or stops calling the junior crew for smaller repairs, I'd write down the dates and compare them month by month. One quiet week could be weather; a repeated pattern would be different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which task would you refuse to leave to the assistant, even if coworkers used it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't let a route score decide whether a pole is safe to climb. I want the crew lead and the person on the ground to look at the actual hardware together.

say: I say a **clean diagram** cannot show a loose branch on the road.
I want the crew to check the **real site** before climbing.
think: I worry the company will leave **junior names** off a smaller roster.
I have little room to replace **lost hours** with another nearby job.
do: Keep using the approved **AI route tool** and learn its features from senior workers.
Request a paid **field qualification** and record monthly callout hours.
feel: I'm **anxious** about roster cuts even though I adapt quickly to useful tools.
S1.quote: I'd say a clean diagram doesn't show the loose branch on the actual road.
fieldNote: He is an early adopter but draws a firm line around **climbing decisions**.
He wants a monthly record to separate a weather lull from **reduced callouts**.

steps.text: Use the approved AI route tool daily and learn its new access features
Continue field shifts while tracking monthly callout hours
Request an additional paid field qualification from the utility

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years doesn't give my family much time to plan around a company decision. The crews may keep working for a while, but the office can cut scheduling and records jobs as soon as AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I won't let a cheap answer decide who climbs a live pole. We need a named person checking the line and the grounding before anybody goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still get field shifts until robots arrive around 2031, but that isn't a promise that this company will keep every crew. My savings are short, and there are few other line jobs nearby if my roster is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the union to seek paid practical training and clear notice before a crew is dropped. In 2028 I wouldn't move into dispatch or records as a safe job, because AGI can do that thinking work. In 2029, if I'm still on the roster, I'd take the company's paid cable-splicing course and keep earning on field jobs while they last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about losing income before the robots arrive, especially with the mortgage and children depending on my pay. I can move fast on training if it is paid, but I don't know what physical work will be safe once robots spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner notice first if your pay started falling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia would see me stop topping up the grocery card and delay replacing the washing machine. We would protect the mortgage and children's school routine before buying anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn quickly, but what if the cable-splicing course costs money or cuts into your shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would ask the employer or union to cover the fee and schedule training hours as paid work. I wouldn't borrow for it while our savings are so low.

say: I say **a person must check** the line and grounding before anyone climbs.
I would ask for **paid notice** before a crew is dropped.
think: I may keep field shifts until **2031**, but the company could cut crews sooner.
I won't treat **dispatch or records** as safe work after AGI.
do: Ask the union for **paid practical training** and notice before crew cuts.
Take the company's paid **cable-splicing course** in 2029 if still rostered.
Protect the mortgage and children's routine before replacing **household goods**.
feel: I'm **anxious** about losing wages while the mortgage and children depend on them.
S2.quote: I'd tell the crew I won't let a cheap answer decide who climbs a live pole.
fieldNote: He expects a short **field-work window** but does not assume the employer will keep crews.
His course plan depends on paid hours because **borrowing is unaffordable**.
He rules out desk duties as a fallback once AGI can do **thinking work**.

steps.text: Ask the union to secure paid notice and practical training before cuts
Take the paid cable-splicing course in 2029 if field shifts remain
Delay replacing the washing machine to protect mortgage payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build a stronger record at the utility before the first change, though I would not count on an office move. Thinking AI comes in 2031 and the hands-on robots in 2034, so field work gets extra time, not permanent protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the extra time should come with paid training and a clear staffing plan. I want to be ready for more complex field repairs, not promised that a certificate keeps robots away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 at AGI and 51 when the robots arrive. I have time to earn a higher practical qualification, but if the utility reduces crews there still may be no local opening to move into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for paid mentoring on fault isolation and cable splicing, and put each signed-off task in my qualification record. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd keep taking field shifts, finish the next practical course if funded, and check published jobs at neighbouring utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but five years gives me some control over how quickly I build skills. I still need wages every month, so a course that takes me off the roster without pay would not work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see in the qualification record before you trusted it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a crew lead to sign each practical task and the company to say which jobs that qualification covers. A badge by itself won't make another utility hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a desk-based planning course as a backup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't call that a backup after AGI can plan and check work. I'd compare actual field vacancies and their pay before moving my family or changing employers.

say: I say **five years** should include paid training and a staffing plan.
I want practical qualifications, not a promise that skills keep **robots away**.
think: I'll be **48** at AGI and **51** when robots arrive.
I may build skills, but there may be **no local opening** if crews shrink.
do: Request paid mentoring in **fault isolation** and cable splicing now.
Keep field shifts in **2032**, finish funded training, and check nearby utility jobs.
feel: I'm **anxious**, but paid mentoring would give me some control over the next five years.
S3.quote: I'd say the extra time should come with paid training and a clear staffing plan.
fieldNote: He converts extra time into **signed-off practical skills**, not desk training.
He would compare actual vacancies and **pay** before changing employers or moving family.
He expects **family responsibilities** to change as his children grow older.

steps.text: Keep taking utility field shifts during the first year after AGI
Complete funded fault-isolation or cable-splicing training in 2032
Check published neighbouring-utility vacancies and pay before moving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me time to finish the qualifications I'm working on and to see how the utility changes its crews. My children will be older before the robots arrive, so I would keep reviewing our family plans as their next steps become clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use those years to get paid training and honest numbers about field staffing. No one can promise the same work will exist when robots arrive, so I wouldn't tell my children that my job is secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when the robots do. That is long enough to build field experience, but I cannot rely on records, planning, or a coding course once AGI can do thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep my qualification record current and ask the utility for paid training dates and staffing forecasts. In 2037, if field shifts continue, I'd compare my wages with the household budget, take employer-paid practical training if offered, and decide what we can put toward the children's next steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning gives me choices, but my savings still cover less than a month today. I'm anxious about current bills and the possibility that a later robot rollout could take away the work I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What family decision would the changing timeline bring forward for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2037 my children will be seventeen and twenty, and I need to plan around their next steps. I'd set a study budget only after I know what my wages and mortgage payments look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would make you decide whether to stay in linework after AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the utility's actual field roster, the wages for any new practical role, and the date of the next paid course. I would not treat an open vacancy or a course as a guarantee that the job lasts through 2039.

say: I say we should use the decade for **paid training** and honest staffing numbers.
I won't tell my children that linework will remain **secure** after 2039.
think: I'll be **53** at AGI and **56** when robots arrive.
My current savings and mortgage keep the longer warning from feeling **safe**.
do: Keep my **qualification record** current and request written staffing forecasts.
Compare actual wages and bills in **2037** before choosing whether to stay.
Set a study budget for my children after checking the **mortgage and pay**.
feel: The warning gives me choices, but **thin savings** make today's bills anxious too.
S4.quote: In 2037 my children will be seventeen and twenty, and I need to plan around their next steps.
fieldNote: He connects the long timeline with the children's **later education choices**.
He asks for a real **roster and wages** rather than a promise of work through 2039.

steps.text: Keep the lineworker qualification record current while working
Take employer-paid practical training in 2037 if available
Set a study budget for the children after reviewing wages and mortgage payments

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots may arrive around 2031 before I have enough saved to manage a layoff. Paid practical training, clear notice, and a way to challenge a cut to junior shifts would help me plan with my partner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I wish you'd asked what happens when a worker reports that a route or site doesn't look right. The crew still owns the safety decision, and I want the system to leave room for us to stop a job.

headlineQuote: The crew still owns the safety decision, and I want the system to leave room for us to stop a job.
portrait: Ivan is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two children and a mortgage.
He adopts digital tools early but keeps **site safety** in the crew's hands.
His **thin savings** and few nearby employers make lost shifts a serious family concern.
He seeks paid practical training while recognizing that **robots may reach** field work later.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most because robots may arrive around 2031 before he has a larger cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **practical training**, clear notice and a way to challenge junior-shift cuts would help him plan.
